question: to the Commission Barbara Bonte (PfE) Subject:

On 24 March 2026, the Commission detected a cyberattack on the cloud infrastructure of the Europa.eu platform. According to CERT-EU, approximately 92 GB of data was stolen, including personal data and email content. In addition, data from at least 29 other EU entities may have been concerned. The attack was carried out via a compromised version of the opensource tool Trivy. This was already the second attack on the Commission in 2026, following an earlier hack in February on the Mobile Device Management platform. These incidents are occurring whilst the Commission itself has proposed a new cybersecurity package and is requiring thousands of public authorities and businesses to comply with the NIS2 Directive and the EU Cybersecurity Regulation. 1.
How does the Commission assess the credibility of its own cybersecurity regulations, in the light of the fact that the institution has been compromised twice in the space of a few months?
What lessons is the Commission drawing from the fact that the attack occurred via a compromised open-source tool in the supply chain?
Who within the Commission bears political and operational responsibility for this, and will the internal review be made public?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) In the present geopolitical context, the Commission is a high-profile target for cyberattacks. Their scenarios are increasingly complex and deceptive, as threat actors use more advanced techniques, including artificial intelligence. This trend is demonstrated by the two recent significant incidents. Neither of them caused any major disruption to the Commission’s IT systems, proving that cybersecurity measures put in place by the Commission in line with Regulation 2023/28411 – and continuously improved in cooperation with CERT-EU2 – are effective in detecting and containing the attack attempts swiftly, and in reducing their impact. A thorough investigation of the personal data breach dimension of both incidents was conducted, in full respect of the regulatory obligations. The incident involving the cloud infrastructure of the europa.eu platform points to a major and growing risk of software supply-chain attacks. The Commission is reinforcing the measures aiming at verification of software origin and authenticity, tighter controls on third-party and open-source components, continuous monitoring, and defence-in-depth to limit the propagation of attacks. Lessons learned from all incidents are systematically used to improve the Commission’s internal operational protocols. Besides, the Commission proposed a new framework to strengthen the security of information and communications technologies supply chains in the revised Cybersecurity Act 23. The roles and responsibilities in cybersecurity in the Commission are defined in the internal cybersecurity risk-management, governance and control framework4, in full compliance with the provisions of Regulation 2023/2841, in particular with regards to reporting obligations.
1 Regulation (EU, Euratom) 2023/2841 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2023

laying down measures for a high common level of cybersecurity at the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the Union, OJ L, 2023/2841, 18.12.2023. 2 The Cybersecurity Service for the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. 3 Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), the European cybersecurity certification framework, and ICT supply chain security and repealing Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (The Cybersecurity Act 2), COM/2026/11 final. 4 Commission Decision (EU, Euratom) 2017/46 of 10 January 2017 on the security of communication and information systems in the European Commission, C/2016/8998.
